comparator.name: Digital Society
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 regulations and faculty outline confirm the English full-time Digital Society BA. Years one and two each contain 60 EC of required study. Year three contains 30 EC of approved electives, 4 EC of research experimentation, 9 EC of controversies and a 17 EC thesis. The third-year mentoring scheme is optional and carries no credits. The electives remain genuine choice space. Progression and assessment follow the regulations.

core: Digital society as an interdisciplinary object of study: how digitalisation transforms culture, politics, the economy and the environment, introduced in What is (a) Digital Society?, Artificial Society and Controversies in Digital Society

Digital cultures, media and the history of ICT: Digital Cultures, Virtual Worlds and ICT Revolutions: Continuity and Change, covering influencers, virtual worlds, emerging media and the historical development of computing
Digital politics, regulation and rights: Digitalisation and Politics and Regulating the Digital, including how governments regulate technology and online safety, privacy and digital rights
Digital ethics: ethical analysis of data, algorithms and generative AI, taught through The 'Good Life' and the programme's ethical-dilemma focus
Digital technologies and critical making: Introduction to Digital Technologies I and II, Critical Making, the basics of coding and cyber security, and designing digital systems for social good

Research methods for digital society: What is Research?, Making Knowledge, Using Digital Sources, Quantitative Data Analysis, Working with Big Data, Qualitative Research Methods and Interdisciplinary Research Design, including data analysis for social questions
Independent research: the Research Experimentation Zone and the 17-EC Bachelor Thesis that concludes the programme
Digital economy, business and organisations: Social and Environmental Impacts of the Digital Economy and the study of digital business, leadership and innovation
Creative digital communication: creating with digital media and formats, from Virtual Worlds to the creative communication that the programme develops
adjacent: Advertised minor directions may contribute to open elective study: arts/heritage, European studies, gender/diversity, globalisation/development, philosophy, healthcare, psychology, entrepreneurship, sustainability, art/law/policy, human/legal decision-making and post-growth cities. Current minor-page applications concern2027–28; these names are not instantiated or guaranteed for the2026–27 reference cohort.
Data, algorithms and AI as technical objects: the science behind generative AI, social-media algorithms and data analysis for social questions
Sustainable digital futures: how digital systems can be designed for environmental and social sustainability, linking technology, people and the planet, sustainability and post-growth society
questions: How do digital technologies, generative AI and social-media algorithms reshape society, behaviour, beliefs and politics, and how can they be used responsibly?
How can digital and technological systems be designed and governed so that they are environmentally and socially sustainable?

trace: introduces the study of film and media, tracing the historical development of cinema and the elements of film form (narrative, cinematography, editing, sound) and treating media as cultural forms that reflect and shape society; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's media and digital-culture analysis by supplying the analytical vocabulary, although its main object is film rather than digital media

studies how pre-digital media technologies such as cassette tapes, typewriters and printed books shaped the production, circulation and preservation of knowledge, through material analysis and historical interpretation; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's history-of-ICT component (ICT Revolutions: Continuity and Change) but addresses earlier media technologies rather than the digital revolution itself

examines how television, film, podcasts and TikTok narratives shape social attitudes and everyday life, treating viral moments as cultural snapshots of contemporary values and anxieties; it directly engages the social-media and digital-culture content of the target's Digital Cultures, although from an American mainstream-media perspective

analyses how film, photography, sound and digital media make ecological processes and environmental risk visible and shape how environmental problems are understood; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the link between media and the planet in the target's technology, people and planet identity

teaches data cleaning, manipulation and visualization for tabular, spatial and text data with hands-on examples from the sciences, social sciences and humanities, and ends in an own research project applying data analysis to a research question; it offers related content for introductory data handling and analysis for social questions, the basis of the target's Working with Big Data and data-science content

teaches structured and object-oriented programming in Python with testing and debugging; it offers a partial contribution to the basics of coding that the programme page names for the target's Introduction to Digital Technologies I, although it is a computer-science gateway course rather than a digital-society course

examines the ethics of AI (fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility and accountability, the moral status of AI systems, existential risk and political implications) together with the psychology of AI; it offers related content for the target's digital-ethics and generative-AI-and-society direction

teaches moral theories (virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism) and practical ethics topics such as poverty, future generations and climate change; it offers related content for the ethical reasoning behind the target's The 'Good Life' and digital-ethics content, but treats ethics generally rather than technology ethics specifically

analyses political systems and democracies, including phenomena such as democratic backsliding, with the theory-driven qualitative and quantitative research tools of political science; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's Digitalisation and Politics by supplying political-science foundations, but has no digital content of its own

covers human-rights law (treaties, monitoring mechanisms, case law) and its historical and philosophical foundations; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's online safety, privacy and digital-rights direction, but treats rights generally rather than digital rights specifically
Analyses policy across local, national and international settings through a sugar-policy case and policy memos. It supplies policy-analysis practice relevant to digital regulation

introduces the concepts, methods and theories of sociology for analysing societies from everyday interactions to long-standing institutions; it supplies the social-science foundation for the target's What is (a) Digital Society? and Artificial Society
Examines civil society, public spheres and digital publics through social theory and empirical group research

teaches the four stages of qualitative research (design and preparation, data collection and management, analysis and interpretation, dissemination); it offers related content for the target's Qualitative Research Methods

teaches research design (operationalization, experimental design, sampling, surveys) and descriptive and inferential statistics including an introduction to multivariate statistics; it offers related content for the research-methods foundation of the target's What is Research? and its quantitative skills
teaches multivariate statistical models (linear regression, factor analysis, ANOVA/ANCOVA, logistic regression); it offers related content for the target's Quantitative Data Analysis
Examines AI in firms and economies, including adoption, labour, inequality, environmental effects and governance
Develops communication through persuasion, framing, nudging and ethical work with community partners
Develops experimental writing and performance, including sonic and digitally mediated forms. It contributes bounded creative practice

teaches predictive modelling (linear regression, classification, resampling, tree-based methods, support vector machines, clustering) with real-world applications; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's Working with Big Data by extending data analysis from description to prediction

trains recognition of misinformation, fake news and cognitive biases, with a historical overview of misinformation in politics and society; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's online-harms and information-literacy themes, but is not specific to digital platforms

teaches algorithm design and analysis with weekly laboratory work, experimental performance analysis and an account of how algorithms have shaped the modern world; it gives the technical understanding of algorithms behind the target's social-media-algorithm and AI content

Calculus, integration, complex numbers and differential equations provide mathematical preparation for the technical alternative,7.5EC. The actual profile does not establish a full linear-algebra curriculum.

introduces relational database systems and SQL (relational theory, normalization, query processing, authorization); it makes a specific complementary contribution to data analysis for social questions by teaching how the data behind digital systems are stored, queried and protected

Internet architecture and protocols, operating-system processes, concurrency, memory and file systems,7.5EC. Genuine technical understanding of digital infrastructure and its control; the official accessible evidence does not establish identical content in Introduction to Digital Technologies II or a dedicated cyber-security curriculum.

builds and trains neural networks and applies them to computer vision, large language models and generative AI in Python; it offers related content for the science behind generative AI named in the target's programme description

provides mathematical statistics (probability theory, distributions, sampling, parameter estimation, simulation); it offers related content for the quantitative foundations of data analysis for social questions at a more theoretical level than the target itself

introduces planning and decision-making techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non-deterministic environments, addressing uncertainty, partial observability and optimizing behaviour under constraints; it offers related content for the technical side of how algorithmic systems decide

examines what drives consumer behaviour and engagement, how customer trust can be built responsibly, and digital and AI-driven marketing; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the question of how algorithms and digital marketing shape behaviour

integrates psychology into economic theory, showing how biases, heuristics and framing shape decisions, with behavioural experiments; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the question of how choice environments and algorithms shape behaviour, but is not specific to digital settings

Search in known/unknown/adversarial environments, constraint satisfaction and experimental optimisation projects include convex optimisation and linear/nonlinear programming,7.5EC. A genuine algorithmic contribution; not dedicated social-media recommender design or complete digital-system critical making.

alternatives.label: Digital Media, Society and AI
alternatives.labelReason: The composition combines media/culture, social and political analysis, ethics and AI governance with programming, data science, machine learning and algorithms. Six advanced courses and whole7.5ECweights were reviewed. Poetry-led Creative Communication Laboratory is replaced with the actual AI search/optimisation course; no virtual-worlds, specialist digital-policy or thesis equivalence is claimed.
alternatives.concept: Study how media, AI and digital systems shape public debate, organisations and everyday life. Combine media analysis and creative work with sociology, AI ethics, economics and policy analysis. Use programming, data analysis and research methods to investigate social questions.
progression: Introductory media and sociology precede advanced study of media narratives and publics. Research Methods & Statistics precedes Statistics & Experimental Methods, and data handling precedes Machine Learning. Programming precedes advanced algorithms and optimisation.
traceOverrides: analyses how film, photography, sound and digital media make ecological processes and environmental risk visible and shape how environmental problems are understood; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's media analysis and to the environmental side of Social and Environmental Impacts of the Digital Economy, although its focus is environmental representation

alternatives.label: Data, Algorithms and AI in Society
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has twelve courses in programming, computer science, AI, data science and mathematics (Introduction to Programming, Mathematical Methods, Introduction to Data Science, Machine Learning, Neural Networks & Deep Learning, AI Ethics, Decision-making in AI, Optimization Methods in AI, Networks & Operating Systems, Database Management Systems, Algorithms & Data Structures and Probability & Statistics), three on research methods and statistics (Research Methods & Statistics, Statistics & Experimental Methods and Qualitative Research Methodology), and eight on the social, ethical and behavioural side (Ethics, Human Rights, Persuasive Communication, From T.V. to TikTok, Media Archaeology, Calling Bullshit, Marketing & Consumer Engagement and Behavioral Economics), plus Personal & Professional Development. The label names the technical majority first and the social and behavioural perspectives second; it does not claim a full computer-science or data-science degree.
alternatives.concept: Study the technologies behind digital life through programming, networks, databases, machine learning and AI. Use media studies, ethics and behavioural economics to ask how these technologies influence choices and participation.
alternatives.distinctness: This option uses 8 different courses to deepen networks, databases, mathematical statistics, AI decision-making and neural networks, and add behavioural economics and digital marketing. The first option devotes more courses to sociology, media interpretation, public policy, creative practice and the social impacts of AI.
progression: Programming precedes networks, algorithms and advanced AI. Mathematical Methods precedes Probability & Statistics and Neural Networks & Deep Learning. Data Science precedes Machine Learning, and Research Methods & Statistics precedes the later applied statistics and behavioural economics courses.
traceOverrides: examines the ethics of AI (fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility and accountability) together with the psychology of AI; it offers related content for the ethical analysis of algorithmic and generative-AI systems that complements the technical courses in this programme

examines how television, film, podcasts and TikTok narratives shape social attitudes and everyday life, treating viral moments as cultural snapshots of contemporary values and anxieties; it directly engages the social-media and digital-culture content of the target's Digital Cultures, although from an American mainstream-media perspective

trains recognition of misinformation, fake news and cognitive biases, with a historical overview of misinformation in politics and society; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's online-harms and information-literacy themes, but is not specific to digital platforms

candidates.label: Data, algorithms and AI as technical objects of digital society
Sustainable digital futures and post-growth society
candidates.reason: Media & the Environment and Business & Economy in the Age of AI offer specific intersections. Sustainability and governance courses add context, while the available study of environmental impacts of digital systems is concentrated in courses already used by the broad option.

candidates.label: Psychology and human decision-making
candidates.reason: Behavioural Economics, Statistics & Experimental Methods and persuasion provide meaningful human-decision study, but the digital application is concentrated in courses already used by the technical option.

candidates.label: Law, policy and rights
candidates.reason: Human Rights, Public Policy Analysis and AI Ethics provide legal, policy and ethical study. Their combination offers limited dedicated digital law, and the closest option already incorporates their strongest contributions.

candidates.label: Arts, heritage and intellectual traditions
candidates.reason: Media Archaeology and Introduction to Film & Media add historical and cultural interpretation. Available heritage and traditions courses have limited digital application beyond the closest option.

candidates.label: European studies, globalisation and development
candidates.reason: European politics and global development offer comparative institutional contexts, with too little sustained digital inquiry for another Digital Society option.

candidates.label: Gender and diversity
candidates.reason: Media & Race and sociology provide ways to study representation and exclusion, while a sustained pathway on digital identity and inequality would rely mainly on courses already used by the closest option.

candidates.label: Entrepreneurship
candidates.reason: Strategy & Digital Transformation, marketing and business AI support applied business study. The available dedicated digital courses largely share the technical or broad option’s questions, while general venture courses would shift the emphasis to business.

candidates.label: Sustainable healthcare
candidates.reason: Biomedical and health courses provide domain context, but the available AI ethics examples do not amount to a sustained digital healthcare curriculum.

candidates.label: Digital systems for social good and creative digital communication
candidates.reason: Creative Communication Laboratory supports creative experimentation and some digital forms. Media analysis and computing contribute different skills, with limited sustained production or civic design for a distinct third option.

candidates.label: Digital leadership, innovation and business transformation
candidates.reason: The strategy course covers planning and digital value, and business AI covers adoption. Together with marketing these make an applied cluster, but specialist depth in organisational digital change is limited and the closest option already addresses the main societal question.

candidates.label: Independent digital-society research
candidates.reason: Quantitative and qualitative research courses offer defensible methods in both options. Independent research is an additional opportunity and cannot justify a distinct taught Digital Society option.

selection.assessment: Two coherent options address different parts of Digital Society. The closest combines social analysis and media with technical study. The second develops computing and data methods in more depth while retaining inquiry into social and ethical effects. The remaining interests either overlap these options or lack sufficient sustained digital-society coverage.

Research methods, statistics and applied research

Research Methods & Statistics teaches research design, sampling, surveys and introductory statistics. It provides related introductory research skills; the methods, assessment and full scope of Maastricht’s 5 EC component are not treated as identical.

Statistics & Experimental Methods teaches multivariate modelling, regression, factor analysis and analysis of variance, with applications to human phenomena. These are related quantitative tools; the courses’ coverage, assessment and EC differ.

Qualitative Research Methodology teaches research design, data collection, interpretation and a group project. It provides related qualitative research skills; the courses’ specific methods, assessment and EC are not treated as identical.

notes.text: UCR offers substantial work in AI, data, media and social analysis. Maastricht integrates these areas through dedicated study of digital politics and regulation, virtual worlds and critical making. UCR’s creative laboratory includes experimental forms, with digital media as one part of that work.

Maastricht requires 120 EC in the first two years. Year three includes 30 EC of approved electives, 4 EC of research experimentation, 9 EC of controversies and a 17 EC individual thesis. UCR’s optional independent research sits outside the displayed 180 EC.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht Digital Society studies how digital technologies shape culture, politics, organisations and everyday life. It combines humanities and social-science analysis with digital skills, data, ethical inquiry and interdisciplinary research. The final year includes approved electives, research experimentation, controversies and an individual thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR option combines media and social analysis with computing, AI and policy. The second focuses on the technical workings of data and AI while examining their social effects. Maastricht brings these areas together in dedicated digital society courses and requires a 17 EC individual thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC includes 120 EC of compulsory study in the first two years. Year three combines 30 EC of approved electives with research experimentation, controversies and a thesis.
